say.text: Two ulcers sit on the first part of the duodenum. One is on the front wall, the other on the back wall. Each will eventually erode through its full thickness.
Predict first: which one is more likely to perforate into the free peritoneal cavity?

choices.label: The front wall ulcer, which faces the free peritoneal cavity
The back wall ulcer, the deeper and more sheltered site
The back wall ulcer, because the artery behind it is the danger
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The front wall opens straight into the free peritoneal cavity, so an ulcer that goes through it spills acid and gastric contents into the abdomen.
Anterior ulcers tend to perforate; posterior ulcers tend to bleed.
Not right. The back wall looks like the deeper, more sheltered site, so it feels like the place a hole would go through.
Ask what lies on the far side of each wall: the open peritoneal cavity, or a major artery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the pairing. Depth is not what decides the outcome.

say.text: Why it fails: the back wall ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds. The front wall ulcer perforates into the free cavity.
Right: the front wall is the commonest perforation site on the first part of the duodenum.
Not right. The artery behind the back wall is the famous one, so it feels as if the artery marks where the danger lies.
Ask what the artery does when it is eroded: does it open the belly, or fill the gut?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two outcomes. The artery explains bleeding, not perforation.

say.text: Why it fails: the artery explains bleeding. Erosion of the gastroduodenal artery bleeds into the gut; it does not open the free peritoneal cavity.
Right: the front wall ulcer perforates, and the back wall ulcer bleeds.
Think about what lies on the far side of each wall, and what each outcome needs.
A perforation needs an open route into the abdomen. Which wall has one?
Now the pair side by side. A back-wall ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds.
A front-wall ulcer perforates into the free peritoneal cavity.
Front opens, back bleeds.
Same two ulcers as before. Why does the back-wall one bleed instead of perforating?

choices.label: The back wall is thinner, so it erodes straight into the cavity
The gastroduodenal artery lies behind the wall, and the ulcer erodes it
The back wall faces the free cavity, so acid makes it bleed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Behind the first part of the duodenum runs the gastroduodenal artery; a back-wall ulcer that erodes it bleeds.
The front wall opens into the free cavity instead, so it perforates.
Not right. A thin wall looks like the one that goes through first, so thickness feels like the deciding factor.
As the ulcer eats through, what does it meet next: an open cavity, or a vessel?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at what lies behind the wall, not how thick it is.

say.text: Why it fails: thickness does not decide the outcome. What lies behind the wall does: an artery for the back wall, the open cavity for the front.
Right: the gastroduodenal artery lies behind the first part, so the back-wall ulcer erodes it and bleeds.
Not right. Acid is what spills, so a wall that seems to face the cavity feels like the one that bleeds.
Ask which wall faces the open cavity, and which wall faces an artery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the reversal is the trap: the wall that faces the cavity is the one that perforates.

say.text: Why it fails: the mechanism is reversed. Acid entering the open cavity marks the front wall as the perforator, and the back wall faces the artery.
Right: the back-wall ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds, because the artery lies behind it.
Think about what the ulcer erodes as it goes through: the open cavity, or a blood vessel.
Which of those causes bleeding, and which leaks into the free peritoneal cavity?
After a perforation the belly passes through three classic stages. Predict the order.
Which order is right, from first to last?

choices.label: Reaction first, then chemical, then bacterial peritonitis
Chemical peritonitis, then reaction, then bacterial peritonitis
Chemical, then bacterial peritonitis, then reaction
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Acid and bile go in first, causing chemical peritonitis.
The exudate then dilutes the irritant, giving the reaction. Bacteria take hold over hours, causing diffuse peritonitis.
Not right. The early calm feels like the opening picture, so reaction seems to come before the acid does.
Ask what enters the belly first: the bacteria, or the stomach's own contents?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the lull comes after the acid, not before it.

say.text: Why it fails: reaction is a lull that follows the acid, not a step before it. Gastric contents enter the belly before any bacteria do.
Right: chemical peritonitis, then reaction, then diffuse bacterial peritonitis.
Not right. Reaction sounds like the body's recovery, so it feels like the last step of the story.
Ask what the lull depends on: the patient's own healing, or the irritant being diluted by exudate?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the reaction is a dilution, not a cure. It sits between the two peritonitides.

say.text: Why it fails: the reaction is not recovery. Exudate dilutes the irritant and the patient seems better, but the bacteria are still arriving.
Right: chemical first, then reaction, then diffuse bacterial peritonitis.
Start with what leaves the stomach. What reaches the belly before any bacteria?
Then ask what the belly does to dilute that first irritant.
Six hours after a sudden perforation, the pain has eased and the patient looks better. The belly is still tender.
Predict: what does this easing mean?

choices.label: Recovery: observe and re-examine in the morning
The reaction phase: the irritant is diluted, bacteria follow
Resolving gastritis: switch to oral antacids
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The easing is the reaction phase: exudate dilutes the irritant, so the pain softens.
Bacteria are still multiplying, and diffuse bacterial peritonitis follows. Reaction is a false calm.
Not right. Less pain and a brighter face look like healing, so recovery feels like the obvious reading.
Ask whether a belly that is still tender has stopped being infected.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the calm is a stage of the disease, not the end of it.

say.text: Why it fails: the calm is the reaction stage, where the diluted irritant hides ongoing peritoneal damage. The bacteria keep growing.
Right: the reaction phase, with bacterial peritonitis to follow. The belly needs urgent action.
Not right. Pain that eases fast feels like gastritis settling, so a gentler antacid seems to fit.
Ask what caused a sudden severe pain in the first place, and whether gastritis does that.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the cause. A hole through the full wall, with acid in the cavity, is not gastritis.

say.text: Why it fails: a perforation is a hole through the full wall, letting acid and bile into the free cavity. It is not inflamed mucosa.
Right: the reaction phase, where the diluted irritant softens the pain before bacteria take over.
Think about what the exudate does to the acid and bile already in the belly.
Does the easing mean the source has gone, or that it is now spread out?
Two patients have severe abdominal pain. One lies motionless with a rigid belly; the other keeps rolling and pacing.
Why does the first one lie still?

choices.label: Movement is blocked by pain in the gut wall, as in colic
Worse pain drives more movement, so stillness means milder pain
Movement jars the inflamed peritoneum and worsens the pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The inflamed peritoneum hurts with each jolt, so the patient keeps still.
Colic is the opposite: a cramping gut eases with movement, so the patient writhes.
Not right. Colic makes people writhe, so the gut wall seems to be what stops movement in any painful belly.
Ask what movement does to an inflamed lining, compared with a cramping gut.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two pictures: colic moves, peritonitis keeps still.

say.text: Why it fails: the stillness comes from the peritoneum, not the gut wall muscle. Movement jars the inflamed lining and makes the pain worse.
Right: the still patient is guarding an inflamed peritoneum. The colicky patient's pain eases with movement.
Not right. Pain feels as if it should scale with movement, so the worst pain seems to mean the most movement.
Ask which patient's pain movement makes worse, and which patient's pain it eases.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the reversal is the trap: in peritonitis, movement makes the pain worse.

say.text: Why it fails: the rule runs the other way. Peritonitis makes movement painful, so the patient keeps still whatever the pain score.
Right: the still, rigid patient has the peritonitis. The rolling patient's colic eases with movement.
Think about what happens to the pain when the patient moves: does it ease or get worse?
Which of the two patients is protecting an inflamed lining?
